title: Horrific lifting injuries (how to prevent them)
summary: A long guide to preventing the career-ending lifting injuries: pec tears, shoulder overuse, knee tendon damage, lower back injuries, biceps tears, abdominal hernias, long thoracic nerve rupture and neck problems. Nearly all of his advice comes from his own near-misses. His view is that injuries are never random; they come from poor preparation, poor programming and ego.
claims: Tendonitis is common and manageable with patience; the injuries to fear are freak ruptures that need reattachment or never heal
Injuries do not just happen: every injury has a cause in something the lifter did, so foresight and experience can prevent them
PED users tear pecs because muscle strength outgrows tendon strength; naturals more often get muscle-belly tears near the armpit
Pec tears come from being stretched through a range of motion the muscle was not prepared for
A severe pec muscle tear rarely heals past 80-85% and keeps re-aggravating; his football line coach said a lineman who tears a pec is never good again
He sprained his right pec by benching only 135 lb without warming up; always warm the pec up even if you lifted the weight last week
Do not train the chest in only one plane (only bench); add flies, dips, push-ups and grip variations so the pec is prepared for other movements
Stretch the pecs deeply under low load (bodyweight or light flies) to train the stretch capacity; it removed his pec-shoulder pain
Ring push-ups are his favorite pec-protection lift: the elbows travel far back and the hands reach chest level, which a bench cannot allow
Beginners who cannot bench comfortably through full range should train that range with an easier pressing mode first
Bench injuries are usually shoulder injuries because the shoulders take over; adjust bench angle, hand placement and arch so the pecs do the work
Touch-and-go benching made his right shoulder protract more each rep until at 24 he could barely raise his arm overhead
Horizontal pressing done too often and too hard wears down the shoulders; vertical pressers rarely get shoulder injuries
Balance horizontal with vertical pressing; many lifters tolerate more horizontal volume once they add overhead work
Benching three times a week, as many novice programs prescribe, is too frequent and causes long-lasting shoulder overuse injuries
Lower bench frequency and replace some pressing with push-ups or cable flies, which grow the chest with less shoulder strain
Count the front delt work from bench, dips and push-ups before adding shoulder volume; a lateral raise often just reveals an overuse injury from benching
Vary grip: a non-powerlifter can do back-off bench work with a close grip to take stress off the shoulders
Overdeveloped front delts with weak side/rear delts and traps invite injury; he shrank his front delts and built rear delts and traps, and his shoulder injuries stopped
Strong upper back and traps hold the shoulders down and back, stabilise the rotator cuff and improve posture
Find your own pressing style for your build instead of copying how a big-chested lifter presses; your own style is usually the shoulder-friendly one
Knee ligament tears (ACL, MCL) need surgery, and reattached tendons are more likely to tear again
Squat stance depends on your hip structure; do not copy Olympic lifters' upright torsos, which suit their femur and torso proportions
He needs a narrow-to-medium stance with toes forward; any other stance has hurt him
About five years ago he tried a Tom Platz narrow, toes-out squat with 275 lb after a break and got severe patellar tendonitis that lasted years
Weak hamstrings cause knee pain because the quads do all the work; hamstring training reinforces the knee and teaches the hip hinge
Squats and conventional deadlifts are not enough hamstring work; a deadlift without a lowering phase gives the hamstrings no stretched negative
Hamstring builders: leg curls, hyperextensions, RDLs and kettlebell swings
If the glutes are weak, Bulgarian split squats and single-leg hip thrusts teach glute activation with knee flexion
He fixed his knee pain by relearning the squat and building big hamstrings and glutes
Do not dive-bomb squats or hack squats; control the bottom of the negative, where knees shoot forward when control is lost
Men should not let the knees cave; push the knees outward, press through the whole foot and keep the knee rigid
Most back problems can be fixed and every one can be prevented with resistance training; avoid surgery
The lower back fatigues easily and recovers slowly; keep it fresh as a stabilising bridge for leg training, not a prime mover
Keep the lumbar spine neutral under load; upper back rounding is acceptable but lumbar flexion is not, partly because it kills leg drive
Wrong training frequency is the main cause of lower back pain: too often causes overuse, too rarely leaves it weak
Burning SI-joint pain after deadlifts is inflammation, not a pump, and signals poor frequency management
He now deadlifts or hip-hinges heavy every two days with zero SI-joint pain thanks to controlled frequency
Deadlifts have a poor stimulus-to-fatigue ratio only when overdone; if they stop you training legs for 5-6 days, switch to RDLs
Keep 2 RIR on squats and deadlifts; take RDLs, leg extensions or lunges to failure instead
Never take good mornings to failure without safeties; never let the low back be in a lift-it-or-snap position
Drop lifts that do not suit your build, e.g. a tall long-legged lifter and conventional deadlifts; he dropped sumo because it hurt his ribs
Tears at the tendon attachment, like biceps tears, do not reattach without surgery and the biceps never looks the same
Biceps tears happen at full elbow extension, where the biceps is weakest; keep the arm slightly bent in all curls
Most biceps tear compilations show PED users or people overstretching on preacher curls
Supinated barbell rows can tear the biceps if the arm overextends at the bottom under heavy back loads
Bodybuilders should never mixed-grip deadlift; use double overhand then straps
If a curl variation gives you tendonitis, swap it; regular curls hurt his shoulders so he uses cross-body pinwheel curls
Biceps tears are usually preceded by years of ignored distal biceps tendonitis; fix it early
Beginners should not start at 12 sets of biceps a week; start at 3 and build to 4 then 6
Abdominal hernias need surgery and can kill via strangulation; men are predisposed but it is not inevitable
Brace by breathing in (nose preferred) and tightening the core as if about to be punched, without sucking in or pushing the belly out
Practice bracing with a bed bridge (upper back on bed, body straight) held as long as possible, then add load
Planks belong in programs for bracing; he puts them in clients' programs although he no longer needs them
Hernias come from fast twisting under load; keep the trunk still during lower body lifts and avoid twisting on one-arm rows and when moving furniture
Stretch the abs too (decline sit-ups) so they handle lengthening; likewise RDLs nearly eliminated hamstring pulls in athletes he advised
Lumbar rounding also puts the abs in a weak position and could contribute to a hernia
Long thoracic nerve rupture causes permanent scapular winging and can happen on uncontrolled dead-hang bottoms of pull-ups
Control the bottom of pull-ups, do not dangle or kip; re-engage the scapula before pulling
Studies he read found pull-ups (especially CrossFit kipping) to be a main source of shoulder injuries besides bench and dips
Dead hangs build the mobility for a full bottom position and decompress the lower back
If pressing or pulling triggers neck pain, warm the neck up every session and keep reps in reserve
Going to failure on overhead press gave him shooting neck pain for days; stopping short of failure with less load fixed it
exercises: let elbows travel back; hands reach chest level
deep low-load pec stretch protects against tears
teaches hinge versus squat; strengthens hamstrings
hamstring and glute builder, friendlier to lower back than deadlift
double overhand then straps; no mixed grip
avoids shoulder pain of regular curls
upper back on bed, body straight, hold
mobility for full bottom position; decompresses spine
